title: Hellgates
author: Outpost
summary: How Hellgates work in the Dragonfire era: Antiquarian's Den entry, the exact IP floors and soft caps for 2v2 and 5v5, the healing debuff, the lava change in Dragonfire Patch 3, and the comp and fight habits that win lethal duos.

children: A Hellgate puts your party and one enemy party in the same demon-filled instance. You clear mobs, the lava starts to rise, and sooner or later the two teams meet. The winners take the reward chest, and in lethal they also loot everything the losers wore. The 2v2 is where most small-scale players learn to fight, because a mistake costs one set and you learn something from it every time.
Older videos describe a different mode. These are the changes that matter, oldest first:

Base loot and fame went up, loot no longer scales with Infamy, and the fame bonus from Infamy dropped from 50% to 20%. The winning team now heals and loses its debuffs after a victory, and the 2v2 Hell buff adds another 10% damage.

The soft cap is the number to build around. A 1,300 IP player in a lethal gate fights at 1,170 (1,100 plus 35% of 200). A 1,000 IP player in a non-lethal gate fights at 910. Every silver spent past the cap buys very little.

Spec still matters below the cap.
Two players at the same item tier do not fight at the same IP if one has the weapon line levelled. Check your real number on the character sheet before you queue.
Enter the Den from the city, pick the mode and queue as a full party. The Den has a bank and a repair station, so gear up there.
You spawn on your side with demon packs between you and the other team. Clear them as you move: they give fame and loot, and a pack on your back is how fights get lost.
The lava rises over time and pushes both teams into a smaller space. Rising Lava stacks stay on you after a knockdown, and molten lava breaks shields.
When the teams meet, the fight decides the run. A knocked-down player stays down for up to 10 minutes, so a 2v1 is usually over.
The winners heal up, get their debuffs cleansed and open the reward chest. In lethal, the losers' gear is on the ground as well.

Kills in Hellgates can drop a Hell Memento kill trophy, and every win builds Antiquarian Standing for the Den's mounts and cosmetics. Hellgates also count toward the Conqueror's Challenge under one merged Hellgates category since Season 31.

Most working duos are a healer with a damage dealer, or two self-sufficient bruisers. With a 35% healing debuff, a healer alone cannot out-heal focused burst, so the healer has to bring crowd control or peel as well.

The 5v5 rewards a frontline that can start a fight and a backline that hits the same target. Bring one healer: the extra Healing Sickness on two-healer teams is there to stop double-healer stall. Rotcaller Staff's Plaguebringer, the strongest anti-heal in 5v5, had its cooldown raised from 30s to 35s in Dragonfire Patch 3, so count that window if you play against it.
Since Dragonfire Patch 3 a player standing in lava takes far more damage from players. Zone the enemy into it and never kite through it yourself.
Pick one target and stay on it.
Two players splitting damage lose to two players focusing.
Kill or lock the healer first
when you can reach them. Most duos lose the moment their healer is under pressure.

Fighting with demons on you is how a good duo loses to an average one.

Healing Potions heal a share of your health that scales with IP, and Dragonfire Patch 4 lowered it at every tier (900 IP: 18% to 16%; 1,100 IP: 22% to 19.5%). Plan on less potion healing than older guides assume.

Start in non-lethal. The fights teach the same lessons and a loss costs only repairs. Move to lethal when you win more than you lose in non-lethal and you can replace your set three or four times. For a week, write down what each set costs and what each run brings home. Price your sets in the

summary: How the Mists work after the Radiant Wilds Patch 3 rework: finding and entering wisps, yellow versus lethal rules, the IP soft cap and healing debuff, Knightfall Abbey blessings, Resource Mists, reaching Brecilien, and the habits that keep a solo player alive.

children: The Mists are short-lived instanced zones for solo players and duos. You follow a wisp in the open world, step through its portal and farm camps, chests and resources while other small parties do the same. After a long quiet stretch, Radiant Wilds Patch 3 (June 2026) rebuilt the rewards, and the Mists are a good solo farm again. They are also the way into Brecilien.

Most players who feel stuck at T6 spend their evenings riding between T7 nodes. Gather the plentiful lower tiers in the matching gear and the unlocks come much sooner.
Five lines exist: wood, ore, fiber, hide and stone. Each levels on its own, and gathering gear only boosts its own resource. Splitting your time early means levelling two lines at half speed.

The Royal Continent holds the blue, yellow and red zones around the Royal Cities. The Outlands are all black. Orange rules exist only in instances: the Depths and the Ancient Lands opened from yellow zones.

In a yellow zone, a player who drops to zero health is knocked down. Your equipped items lose 5% durability, and a little system-generated silver drops by your body. Nothing leaves your inventory. Since the Abyssal Depths update a PvP knockdown in a yellow zone lasts

Since Dragonfire, if you have been knocked down for more than 30 seconds in a blue or yellow zone, you can respawn at the nearest region entrance. Outlaws, players in faction combat and players inside an open-PvP subzone cannot.
Yellow zones are where to practise PvP for the cost of repairs.

Red zones use the same flag, but a player who loses dies. Everything you wear and carry drops; some items are destroyed and the rest is lootable. You respawn with nothing at your home or the last city you visited. For a gatherer or hauler, red zones are the first real risk on the Royal Continent, and every road into Caerleon crosses them.

Since Radiant Wilds, several old underground passages between yellow and red zones are now direct region exits (for example Willowsigh Marsh to Darkground Swamp, and Yew Wood to Owlsong Glen). Red zones are closer to safe zones than they used to be, so read the zone colour at every exit.

Thirty voices, a caller shouting abilities and a fight that is over in forty seconds. You do not need to understand all of it. title: Your first PvE build
author: Outpost
summary: How to pick a first solo PvE build that clears packs, heals itself and gets away, why one weapon line beats three, what the 1,200 IP soft cap and the Dragonfire mob changes mean for your gear, and how to find, price and save a tested loadout on Outpost.

toc.title: The three tests every solo build must pass
Choose a weapon line and stay on it
What the current rules mean for your gear
Find a tested loadout on Outpost
Save your version and take it out

children: Your first solo set has three jobs. It kills packs of three to six mobs without stopping to rest, it keeps you alive without a healer, and it costs little enough that a death costs you one evening of farming at most. Everything below is about meeting those three jobs on a budget, in content that rewards you for it.
The three tests every solo build must pass
Hold any build you find up against these before you buy a single piece.

Most open-world camps, solo dungeon rooms and Corrupted Dungeon corridors are packs. A weapon that hits one target clears bosses fine and everything else slowly, and slow clears are where solo players lose their silver per hour.
Lifesteal, a self-heal, a shield or a strong defensive cooldown. Without one you stop after every second pull to eat health back.
A dash, a speed burst or a purge. In a yellow zone it saves you from a bad pull. In the Mists or a Corrupted Dungeon it saves you from another player.
Few weapons pass all three. Let the armor fill the gap: a weapon with no sustain wants a healing chest or helmet, a weapon with no mobility wants boots with a dash or speed.
Choose a weapon line and stay on it
sets how strong a piece is. Tier, enchantment and quality raise it. So does
on the Destiny Board: levels you put into one weapon's specialist node add IP to that weapon, and its mastery levels add IP to every weapon in the same line.

That is why switching lines hurts. A player with a month in Fire Staff hits much harder with a Fire Staff than with the Sword they picked up yesterday at the same tier. Pick a line you enjoy, give it a few weeks, and spend your fame and Learning Points there. Since the Abyssal Depths update, Learning Points work through
: fame on a node with Quick Learn active is multiplied by five while the points drain. Turn it on for the one node you care about, not the whole board. The
keeps a record of your levels.
Large area damage and many tested rotations. Dragonfire raised the Hoarfrost Staff's Avalanche damage and halved its knockback against mobs to help solo clears.
Cloth armor and no self-heal of their own; you need the armor to cover sustain.
Sturdy melee lines, cheap at low tiers, good sustain options.
Dragonfire made the axe Adrenaline Boost expire if you stop hitting an enemy for 3 seconds.
Range keeps you out of most mob mechanics.
You have to kite, and kiting into a second pack is how bow players die.
Slow kills, very hard to kill you.
Clear speed. Fine for learning, weak for silver per hour later.
The Bloodmoon Staff is the most liked solo farming build in the library.
Radiant Wilds Patch 2 halved Tear Open's Blood Pool heal (61 to 30), so it leans more on armor sustain now.
Popular solo builds move with each balance patch. Check what players run this month before you trust a video from two seasons ago. The in-game
helps here: since Radiant Wilds it ranks builds by real gameplay data, and since Dragonfire it shows per-hour damage, healing, kills and deaths with each build's average IP.
What the current rules mean for your gear
Three changes from the last year decide how much gear you should buy.

Since Abyssal Depths, blue and yellow open-world zones, their static dungeons, yellow Mists and Knightfall Abbeys mirroring them soft-cap Item Power at 1,200, keeping only 20% of anything above it. Randomized dungeons ignore the cap. Paying for 1,400 IP to farm a yellow zone wastes most of the extra silver.

Dragonfire cut the most damage reduction you can stack on a mob from 80% to 50%, and the health reduction from 50% to 25%. Single abilities came down with it: Guardian Armor's Enfeeble Aura went from 60% to 25% against mobs, Mercenary Hood's Howl from 30% to 20%. Builds that relied on debuffing mobs into harmlessness now need real sustain.

Knockdown in yellow zones lasts 90 seconds. After 30 seconds knocked down in a blue or yellow open-world region you can respawn at the nearest region entrance, unless you are an outlaw, in Faction Warfare combat or in an open-PvP area. Durability loss and repair costs also scale down when a cap lowers your item's power.
Find a tested loadout on Outpost
Narrow it to a weapon you have specced or plan to spec.
Read the description: the content it was made for, the IP the author aimed for and the rotation.
Check every slot against your budget. A set full of artifact pieces is no use if you cannot replace it twice.

Food is a long buff and the potion is your emergency button. Most solo builds list both. A

is the usual starter potion. Dragonfire Patch 4 (2 November 2026) cut Healing Potion healing at every IP level, more at the top: 16% to 14% at 800 IP, 24% to 21% at 1,200 IP. If a build was tuned around the old potion, expect to need one more piece of sustain. Buy enough for the whole session before you leave town, because riding back for one potion costs more than the potion. Eat before the first pull, not after the first bad one.

Buy one set to wear and keep the silver for a second. A death that leaves you with nothing to wear stops your farming for a day, and the second set is what lets you play without fear.

summary: How to farm Corrupted Dungeons for chests and fame while avoiding the PvP: entry IP for Hunter, Stalker and Slayer, the four-chest route, boss bar point counts, breaking Demonic Shards to banish an invader, and the patch changes that shape the mode in Season 34.

toc.title: Changes that shape the mode now

children: A Corrupted Dungeon is a solo instance where another player can be matched in to hunt you. "Ratting" means you go in for the mobs and chests, and when an invader arrives you banish them instead of fighting. Played well it is one of the steadiest solo silver farms in the game, and most of your runs end without trading a single blow.
You can enter from the Antiquarian's Den in any royal city or from open-world entrances. Since Abyssal Depths the requirement checks your
Item Power, not your average with food and spec bonuses.

is your Corrupted rating. It unlocks Slayer and gives at most 20% extra fame, but since Abyssal Depths it no longer makes chests richer. Base loot and fame went up at the same time to make up for it, so a fresh character's chests match a veteran's at the same difficulty. Both lethal tiers soft-cap Item Power, so the last hundred IP on a set costs far more than it adds. Read the cap in the entrance panel before you pay for it.
Changes that shape the mode now

entry from the Antiquarian's Den, faster matchmaking, PvP in Corrupted Dungeons counts toward Antiquarian Standing, map items salvage for 100% of their value, and you heal and lose debuffs after a win.
Book Chests and Hidden Treasures were removed. Every treasure spawn is now a Treasure Chest.

author: Outpost
summary: How to gather in the Outlands and keep most of what you pick up: a set you can afford to lose, mount carry weights from game data, basing from a Smuggler's Den, the patch changes that matter to gatherers, how to spot a scout early and an escape you can drill until it is automatic.

toc.title: Decide three numbers at the bank

children: The best nodes in Albion, high tier and high enchantment, sit in the black zones of the Outlands. So do the players who hunt gatherers. Anyone there can kill you and take everything you wear and carry. You will lose sets. The skill is losing them rarely and cheaply, and banking often enough that good trips pay for bad ones.
Decide three numbers at the bank
Bring a set and mount you could replace ten times over. If losing it would make you play scared, step it down a tier.

Thirty minutes, an hour, longer. It decides the mount and how much food you pack.
Write them down. Every bad gathering death starts with "one more node" past the threshold.
Your set has two jobs: raise yield on the resource you came for, and buy enough time to remount after a dismount.

Short, valuable trips near an exit

Capacity only helps if you fill it, and a big mounted capacity turns into a trap the moment the mount dies and you are suddenly overweight on foot. The Gallant Horse's charge and the Direboar's invisibility both put your boots on cooldown, so use them only when the escape they buy right now is worth it. Realm Divided raised the carry weight of Salamander mounts, which now compete as gathering mounts. Mount prices move, so check them in the

Rogue Frontier moved Outlands banking into

Outlaws and players in combat cannot enter.
A den is the closest thing to a safe door in the black zone, and you can ride in and mount up inside.

links every den and Outlands Rest market into one book. You can buy from a distant den for a distance fee paid by whoever completes the trade, with no Premium discount. The market shows the distance column and has a Max Distance filter; prices include the fee by default.
You share the den with everyone, gankers included. Watch the exit before you ride out with a full bag.

Guild territories and hideouts work as bases too, with closer exits and friends nearby, but your guildmates compete for the same nodes. A portal town suits a planned trip to one biome, at the cost of longer rides.
Level one line to T8 first.
Wear that resource's gear and gather plentiful T4 to T6 nodes. Steady common nodes level you faster than rare T7 and T8 spawns.
once lines are high: roam T6 to T8 zones, chase enchanted nodes and bring every tool you have levelled.
Check the middle of each map. Most gatherers hug the edges, so central nodes see less traffic.
Do not wait at an empty T7 or T8 node. Respawn times vary too much for camping to pay.

Check the region's player count on the map. The Outlands show 16 to 30 and 31 to 50 as separate ranges, and a crowd you cannot explain is a reason to leave.

A scout keeps eyes on you while friends move in off-screen. Treat a player as a scout if they copy two of your direction changes, ride beside you instead of passing, wait between you and an exit, or ride ahead and come back. You need no proof to leave.

A player on foot with no mount health bar near you is a reason to turn away now.
Keep game sound on. You can hear a dismount or an Invisibility Potion nearby.
Since Realm Divided Patch 3, Smokebomb's invisibility ends when its user interacts with the world, so nobody can sit hidden on a node.
On a big node, remount every so often. You miss the warning while you stay on foot.
Do not ride a straight line to the obvious exit. If the first chaser comes from ahead, the route you already cleared is often safer.

Drill the sequence in a safe zone until your fingers know it, and after a lost escape, look for the first warning you missed. Logging out only ends a trip after the gankers have lost you: your character stays in the world until the timer ends, and taking damage cancels it.

title: Ancient Lands
author: Outpost
summary: How an Ancient Lands run works after Dragonfire Patch 4: portal sizes, lock times and entry windows, orange versus black rules and Item Freeze, island quests and Leygate Keystones, Spirit Essence, the four Drakes and the Fire Drake, Bleedout, and when to extract.

toc.title: The four Drakes and the Fire Drake
Getting out and what the loot is for

children: The Ancient Lands are floating islands above Albion, linked by

. You enter through a portal, clear islands for loot, and leave before someone takes it from you. Every group starts alone, every route you open shows on everyone's map, and the best rewards sit in the middle. Portals appear in the open world and show on the World Map from any distance since Patch 1. A new portal is locked for a while, then stays open for a short entry window.

title: Market flipping
author: Outpost
summary: Buy with buy orders, resell with sell orders and keep the gap. What each step costs with and without Premium, the break-even spread for every buy and sell method, how to pick items with real volume, how to outbid and undercut without feeding a bidding war, and how to check a flip in Outpost before you commit silver.

toc.title: Pick items that trade every day

children: Flipping is the quiet way to make silver from the market itself. You post a buy order under what the item sells for, wait for a seller to fill it, then list it higher. No gathering, no combat and no road. The risk is arithmetic: forget one fee and a flip that looked like 8% profit is a loss.

Instant sale into a buy order

The order window shows the exact silver before you confirm, so check it once against this table on your server. Setup fees are not refunded when you cancel or the order expires. The silver for a buy order is held from the moment you post it, which is why a flipper's real limit is how much silver they can tie up at once.

A seller fills it and the item lands in your market box.
It sells. With Premium the game keeps 4% tax (11,600); without, 8% (23,200).

The spread is the gap between what you pay and what you sell for, as a share of what you pay. Below these numbers the flip loses money before you even count price drops:

Each figure is (1 + buy fee) ÷ (1 − tax − sell fee) − 1. The last row is the classic order-to-order flip, and it needs almost a 10% gap with Premium. Every relist adds 2.5% of the listing to your cost, so a flip that needs two price changes needs another 5% of room.
Pick items that trade every day
A wide gap on an item that sells twice a week is a trap. You sit on the stock while the price drifts. Look for:
The in-game sales history shows what buyers paid and how many sold. Ten sales a day beats one big sale a week.
The item details window shows an estimated market value, per item and for the stack since Radiant Wilds. Bid under it, sell near it.
A gap bigger than your break-even.
If the top buy order and the lowest sell order are closer than the table above, move on.
You will spot a bad price on gear you wear faster than on a recipe you have never crafted.

When another flipper tops your buy order by one silver, answering with one silver starts a bidding war where you both pay the setup fee every round. Raise yours by 5 to 10% in one move instead. Your order goes first in line for the next seller, and many flippers drop an item once someone shows they will pay for it. When the competition goes quiet, cancel and repost lower to keep buying cheap. Count each repost as 2.5% of the order.
On the selling side, list just under the cheapest offer. Round prices read cheaper in a list: 7,989,000 looks lower than 8,021,938, and 999 looks lower than 1,000 for one silver of difference.
Undercut by a little. Dropping 10% under the market to sell faster hands your profit to the buyer, and it resets the price for everyone, including your next batch.
Spread silver across several items so one slow seller does not freeze your bankroll.
Keep a list of your open orders and their prices. The market box fills while you are offline.
Recheck before you relist. If the price fell under your cost, wait or take the small loss early.
Flip in one city first. Cross-city trades add the road;
Buy orders can also stock your own crafting at a discount. A crafter who never buys instantly saves the spread on every material.

toc.title: What returns and what never does

children: Every craft and refine hands back part of the materials you put in. That share is the

and turns it into a return rate once:
A bonus of 18 gives 18 ÷ 118 = 15.25%. Bonuses add first and the formula runs once, which is why a city bonus plus focus gives less than the two rates added together.

Islands, hideouts and other stations outside the royal cities use their own values, so read the station's rate in game before you plan around them. The calculators'

What returns and what never does
Artifacts, faction tokens and enchanting materials (runes, souls, relics) never do

The same goes for the faction-heart refining recipes. A T6 bar can be made from three Runite Ore, a T5 bar and a Mountainheart instead of four ore and a bar; the heart never returns, so only the ore and bar benefit from your rate. Outpost's
calculators leave non-returnable inputs out of the return whatever you tick.

Each recipe has a base focus cost: 54 for a T4 bar, 94 for T5, 164 for T6, 287 for T7 and 503 for T8 in Outpost's recipe data.

For refining, each level in any tier of a resource's refining line (for example Master Ore Smelter) adds 30 efficiency to every tier of that resource, and each level in the tier you are refining adds 250 more. A player with only Master Ore Smelter at 100 has 28,000 efficiency for T6 bars, so a T6 bar costs 164 ÷ 2^2.8 ≈ 23.5 focus, and a day's 10,000 focus covers about 425 bars. All five tiers at 100 reach 40,000 for each tier, a sixteenth of the base cost.
Crafting works the same way with different weights. A specialist node gives its own item the large share and its siblings a smaller one, and Dragonfire changed two of those sibling shares:
15 to 12.5 efficiency per sibling level, and quality bonus 0.375 to 0.3125, to make room for the Dragonslayer set.

Watch the daily bonuses. Saving focus for a +20 day in your refining city adds about four points of return over a normal day.

title: Reading market prices
author: Outpost
summary: What the lowest sell order and the highest buy order tell you, why server, tier, enchantment, quality, city and the age of a price matter as much as the number, where Outpost's prices come from, and why an unavailable price is never zero.

toc.title: The two sides of the book
Match the item before you compare
Check how old the price is

children: Every item in every city has two prices: what sellers ask and what buyers offer. Most bad trades come from reading the wrong one, comparing two different items, or trusting a price that was true yesterday. The
shows both sides for one item in every city, each with the time it was seen.
The two sides of the book
is the cheapest price any seller is asking. Buy instantly and you pay this.
is the best price any buyer is offering. Sell instantly and you get this.
The gap between them is the

. The Market Explorer shows it as sell minus buy, as a share of the buy price. Instant trades give the spread away for speed. Orders capture it and cost you time plus a 2.5% setup fee each, and every sale pays 4% tax with Premium or 8% without. An order-to-order flip needs a spread of about 9.6% with Premium just to break even, which the
Match the item before you compare
Two prices only compare when everything else matches:
Europe, Americas and Asia are separate economies. Outpost's region switch changes every price on the page.
A T6.1 sword and a T6 sword are different items with different books. In item IDs the enchantment follows an @: T6_MAIN_SWORD is the flat Broadsword, T6_MAIN_SWORD@1 the 6.1.
Normal, Good, Outstanding, Excellent and Masterpiece each trade separately. A Masterpiece listing tells you nothing about the Normal price.
Each royal city, Brecilien and Caerleon keep separate books, and the Black Market in Caerleon is its own buyer. The Outlands' Smuggler's Network is another separate market, linked across every den.

Outpost keeps each price with its own city, quality and side of the book, and never blends a Lymhurst sell order with a Martlock buy order into one figure. When the quality you asked for has no data, it shows the other qualities beside it with their own city and time instead of swapping one in.
Check how old the price is
A price is a snapshot of the moment someone saw it. A sell order seen ten minutes ago is a good guide. One seen two days ago may have filled, been cancelled or been undercut.
In the Market Explorer every price carries its age, and the exact UTC time on hover. Anything older than an hour gets a

chip, and the city table's header tells you how many orders are older than an hour. Buy and sell sides keep separate times, so a fresh sell order can sit next to a stale buy order for the same item in the same city. If the cheaper city's price is much older, treat the comparison as a guess and confirm it in game before you ride across the map.
to see how the average moved over the last 7 or 30 days. One spike in a quiet market is often a single sale, not a new price.
When nobody has uploaded a price for an item in a city, Outpost shows a dash and

. It means there is no data. It does not mean the item is free, and it does not prove the market is empty. A price observed as 0 is treated the same way. Calculators keep a result unavailable when any input is missing, so a gap never turns into a fake profit, and a price you type yourself is labelled as yours.

with a client that reads the market windows they open. Busy items in busy cities update often. Rare items, quiet cities and the Asia server can go a long time between uploads, and exact-quality T8 gaps are common. The data is crowd-sourced and comes with no guarantee.

A listing does not prove stock or volume. The order may hold a single item, or another player may take it first. For anything expensive, open the market in game and confirm the order before you spend silver. The game's own item details window has shown an estimated market value per item and per stack since Radiant Wilds, a useful second opinion.

The Black Market in Caerleon buys equipment and hands it out as loot to mobs and chests across the world. It only buys, so in Outpost its price is a buy order you can sell into, never a price you can buy at. A sale there pays sales tax and no setup fee, because you sell instantly. Its demand moves with what players loot and lose, so a high Black Market price on a niche item can vanish after a few sales. Check the time on it like any other price, and compare it with the Caerleon market's own buy orders before you craft for it.

title: Real profit
author: Outpost
summary: How to cost a trade or a craft so the profit holds up in game: purchase price, setup fees, sales tax with and without Premium, the trip between cities, margin against return on investment, station fees, and which returned materials to count, with worked examples you can repeat in Outpost.

toc.title: Crafting and refining: returns and two kinds of profit
Your typed prices stay marked as yours

children: Sell price minus buy price is the number everyone sees first, and it is always too high. A trade is profitable only after every fee, tax and trip is counted. Outpost's calculators ask for each cost on its own line so none slips through. This is what goes on each line.

What it costs to move them
, if the buy and sell cities differ.
Instant buy from a sell order
Instant sale to the Black Market

Selling instantly into a buy order skips the sell setup fee but still pays tax. The game keeps setup fees when you cancel, so each relist pays again. Outpost does not assume your rates: the trade check, transport and production tools start tax and setup at 0, so type 4 and 2.5 (or 8 and 2.5 without Premium) yourself. The route scanner on the flipping page is the exception and starts at 4 and 2.5.
You buy 10 items with a buy order at 10,000 each and sell them with sell orders at 12,000, with Premium.
The raw gap was 20,000 and the fees took more than half. Without Premium the tax is 9,600 and the profit falls to 4,900. In
, type the two prices and the quantity, set the purchase order fee, sales tax and sell order setup fee, and you get the same 9,700 along with the
Outpost shows both, and they divide by different numbers:
= profit ÷ what you sold for. Here 9,700 ÷ 120,000 = 8.1%.

Return tells you where to put limited silver: a 9.5% flip that turns over in a day beats a 20% flip that sits for a week. Margin tells you how much room you have if the price drops before you sell. A thin margin on a volatile item is the trade most likely to turn into a loss.

Buying in one city and selling in another adds the trip: mount upkeep, repairs, any travel cost and a risk allowance for what you might lose. The risk allowance is the chance of losing a load times its value. A 2,000,000 silver load on a red-zone road you lose one time in ten carries 200,000 of expected loss per run, and that belongs in the sum. The
splits a load into trips by weight and adds the cost per trip and the risk you choose.
explains how to pick that number.
Crafting and refining: returns and two kinds of profit
Crafting and refining hand back part of your materials. That return has real value, but you only see it as silver when you use or sell the returned materials. The
calculators split the result in two:
silver in minus silver out for this run, before returned materials.
what the returned materials are worth at your prices.
Outpost's reference case: a craft sells for 3,000, its materials cost 2,000, they return at 20%, the station charges 100 and tax plus setup come to 10% of the sale.

Use upfront silver to check you can afford the run and cash profit to judge it if you will sell the returns cheaply or not at all. Total profit is right only if you reuse or sell the returned materials at the prices you entered.

You choose which materials count toward returns. Artifacts, faction tokens, enchanting runes, souls and relics and Dragon Blood never return, so the tools leave them out whatever you tick. Player-run stations charge a fee per craft, which goes in
; fixed silver costs written into a recipe are added on their own line as

covers how the rate is set.
Your typed prices stay marked as yours

The production and transport tools load market prices where they exist, each with the city and time it was seen. When you type your own price, the tool marks it as yours and keeps it apart from loaded prices; refreshing the market does not overwrite it. If an ingredient or output has no price at all, the result stays unavailable instead of treating the gap as zero.

Example: a five-player group dungeon comp

children: A comp is the plan for a whole party: who plays what, in which gear, with which swaps. Writing it down before the content saves the first ten minutes of every run, and it stops the classic problem of three people arriving as DPS and nobody as tank.
Pick a size the content allows

Realm Divided Patch 3 raised the healing debuff to 35% in 2v2 Hellgates, duo Mists and the Depths, and to 40% in Corrupted Dungeons and solo Mists. Dragonfire removed it from every weapon as a seasonal test to push ZvZ away from plate melee DPS. Melee-heavy ZvZ comps lost their main tool against tanky frontlines, so expect more ranged and caster DPS in big fights.

Dragonfire cut the most damage reduction a group can stack on a mob from 80% to 50% and the health reduction from 50% to 25%. Two debuff supports in a PvE comp now overlap more than before; one, plus more damage, is often better.
